extracted.intended_audience: Practitioners authorized to practice before the USPTO (trademark attorneys/agents) and persons advising them
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and required practices for trademark practitioners presenting papers to the USPTO, including account use, signature rules, reasonable inquiry obligations, and disciplinary/probation conditions following violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (37 C.F.R. § 2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives: (a) increase compliance with U.S. trademark law and USPTO regulations; (b) improve accuracy of trademark submissions; and (c) safeguard integrity of the U.S. trademark register. See Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 Fed. Reg. 31498 (July 2, 2019), and TMEP § 601.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO.gov account required and two-step authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: A USPTO.gov account is required for trademark documents to be electronically filed with the USPTO via the USPTO's electronic filing system; a two-step authentication method is required to access the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process to apply and be granted an account has changed over time; users must accept the USPTO Website Terms of Use when registering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account holder responsibility for confidentiality and activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Account holders are responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of their account information, and for all activities that occur under their account; must log off at end of each session and immediately notify USPTO of unauthorized use or security breach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO Website Terms of Use language: 'You are responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of your account information, and for all activities that occur under your account.' Failure to follow may result in termination, deactivation, limitation, or suspension of account privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark Verified USPTO.gov Account – prohibition on facilitating unauthorized practice of law
rubrics_metrics.description: The trademark verified USPTO.gov account agreement requires that the account 'will not be used to engage in or facilitate the unauthorized practice of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must assent to Trademark Account Agreement terms when obtaining a trademark verified USPTO.gov account (available as of Jan 8, 2022).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account non-transferability and single-account rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark verified USPTO.gov account is not transferable to any other individual or entity and an individual person may only use one trademark verified USPTO.gov account and will not request additional accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Trademark Account Agreement explicitly states accounts are solely for use by the individual whose verified identity is associated with the account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on permitting others to use account credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not permit others to use their trademark verified USPTO.gov account login credentials and must take reasonable steps to prevent others from learning their account login information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement requires prompt notification to USPTO if login credentials have been used by others; sharing credentials may result in temporary or permanent suspension of account privileges. Example: allowing a third-party employee to use credentials to generate ESIGN-ON links violates this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsoring accounts for non-practitioner support staff
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner may sponsor a separate USPTO.gov account for each of their non-practitioner support staff who are directly employed or retained by them (or their firm) and who work under their direct supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsorship is the authorized method to enable staff access rather than sharing the practitioner's own credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193, 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; an electronic signature must be personally entered (combination of letters, numbers, spaces, punctuation) placed between two forward slashes in the signature block.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person may not delegate authority to sign; no person may sign or enter the name of another. Typing another's electronic signature or using document-signing software to generate a signatory's signature is not a valid signature. See TMEP § 611.01(c) and cited cases (e.g., In re Zhang).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submissions signed by someone other than the named signatory are improperly executed
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark submission signed by a person other than the named signatory is improperly executed and cannot be relied upon to support registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited precedents: In re Yusha Zhang; Ex parte Hipkins; In re Cowan. Signature issues can be substantive and may adversely affect rights and the integrity of the registration process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications when presenting papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting any paper to the USPTO (signing, filing, submitting, or later advocating), a practitioner certifies statements made on their knowledge are true and statements on information and belief are believed to be true, and that they have conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific certifications include: (i) paper is not presented for an improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or nonfrivolous argument; (iii) factual allegations have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable investigation; (iv) denials are warranted on evidence or reasonably based on lack of information. See 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inquiry requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must conduct an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances that supports the factual assertions set forth in the paper presented to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to undertake a reasonable inquiry (e.g., into specimens' authenticity or factual support) can violate § 11.18(b)(2) and be grounds for discipline; the document stresses that 'a practitioner...certifies that he or she has conducted an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting a document that includes false, misleading, fictitious, or fraudulent information or representations violates 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1) and may be subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. § 1001.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include false domicile information, signatory information, or claims of use. Violations may jeopardize probative value of filings and lead to disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark use in commerce requirement (15 U.S.C. § 1127; TMEP § 901.01)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mark must be in bona fide use in the ordinary course of trade to support registration; 'use in commerce' requires placement of the mark on goods/containers/displays/tags and that the goods are sold or transported in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use made merely to reserve a right in a mark does not meet statutory standard. See TMEP § 901.02 and case law (Aycock Engr., Inc. v. Airjlite, Inc.). If not in use as of relevant date, registration may be subject to cancellation (see 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.92(f)(2), 2.93, 2.94).

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and scrutiny of specimens of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should verify that specimens submitted to show use in commerce are reliable and not digitally altered; if specimens appear altered, the practitioner should perform a reasonable inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document cites multiple Office actions where specimens were identified as digitally altered and criticizes instances where practitioner spent less than five minutes reviewing applications. Guidance: accept only website specimens from verifiable and well-known websites and check for digital alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation to a client, which includes understanding applicable rules and the terms/conditions of USPTO.gov account agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to understand account terms (e.g., permitting others to use account) is cited as an example of failing to provide competent representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must act with reasonable diligence in representing a client, including conducting reasonable inquiries about specimens and not permitting improper account use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically cited examples: not conducting reasonable inquiry regarding specimens and permitting others to use USPTO.gov account to present documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to integrity of federal trademark registration process (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the integrity of the federal trademark registration process (e.g., not complying with account terms or failing reasonable inquiry) is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include allowing third parties to use one's account and presenting potentially unreliable specimens without adequate inquiry; such conduct supports disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner expectation to know rules and potential disciplinary consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners representing applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO are reasonably expected to know (a) applicable trademark prosecution rules, (b) USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct provisions implicated, and (c) potential disciplinary consequences when those provisions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO publishes ample, readily available information (e.g., TMEP, USPTO trademark webpages) and past disciplinary orders are public; ignorance is not an excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation: contact information notification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, the practitioner must notify the OED Director in writing within 21 days of the Final Order of a postal address, an email address, and a telephone number for correspondence; and must notify of any change within 30 days of that change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are express probation conditions to facilitate OED correspondence and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation: active monitoring/search and reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of probation, the practitioner must: (1) at least bi-weekly search the USPTO online trademark search system for trademark applications identifying them as attorney of record (search format: AT: firstname AND AT: lastname AND FD: [YYYYMMDD TO YYYYMMDD]); and (2) promptly inform the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of each trademark document identifying them as attorney of record that was filed without their knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additionally, practitioner must, at least every two months, submit a written report to the OED Director stating completion of bi-weekly searches and either (A) that no unauthorized filings were identified, or (B) providing copies of correspondence sent to OTEP identifying unauthorized filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation: training requirement (Trademark Basics Boot Camp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to termination of probation, the practitioner must provide a written declaration that they have enrolled in, virtually attended, and completed each of the eight modules comprising the USPTO's Trademark Basics Boot Camp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The declaration must be in compliance with 28 U.S.C. § 1746 (signed statement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation: cooperation with OED and inquiries into third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future inquiry into any third-party entities or persons with whom the practitioner worked or was solicited to work in connection with patent or trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation includes providing information and responding to inquiries about third-party relationships (e.g., foreign representatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement agreement and practice changes with third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner shall revise engagement agreements and practices with third-party entities to (1) limit referral volume; (2) require third parties to check for digitally-altered specimens; (3) accept only verifiable/well-known website specimens; (4) verify clients actually sign documents; (5) ensure clients receive documents and translations they understand; and (6) distribute USPTO rule and signature guidance to third-party employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific revisions in Mr. Olive's agreement include reducing incoming referral volume to no more than fifteen (15) applications per week and distributing information on the U.S. Counsel Rule, USPTO signature rules, account agreements, and certification obligations under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18 to third-party personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement procedure for probation violations (Order to Show Cause and possible suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: If OED Director in good faith believes the practitioner failed to comply with any provision of the Agreement, Final Order, or USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct during probation, the OED Director shall issue an Order to Show Cause and may request the USPTO Director enter an order immediately suspending the practitioner for up to six months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order to Show Cause is served at last address of record; practitioner has fifteen (15) days to respond; if after response OED still believes violation occurred, OED sends materials to USPTO Director to request immediate suspension for up to six months. Practitioner may seek review but suspension is not stayed by review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of disciplinary outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in the OED's electronic FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the Final Order's content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public posting of orders and notices is routine; disciplinary records may be considered in future proceedings as aggravating factors or to rebut statements by the practitioner.
